## Compute (wall − startup; the `startup` row is wall)

**Columns run fastest → slowest** — generated from each table's score row, so the header order
always matches the data. **Bold** = Brood. The suite is split into separate tables because not
every row compares the same thing: one 8-column table would let a data-structure choice or a
native library read as a runtime result.

### Like-for-like — same algorithm, same data structures

Every language expresses these the same way, so the ordering is a runtime comparison.

In `vs best` / `vs avg`, **`+` is slower, `−` is faster**. Rank and distance often disagree:
`reduce` is 2/8 but +7.7× off the best, while `collatz` is 3/8 at only +2.2×.

**<sup>C</sup> C runs 12 of these 15 rows** (`—` marks the three it does not: `errors`,
`errors-deep`, `pipeline`), so Brood's rank column reads out of 9 on the rows C runs and out of 8
on the rest. C is a floor reference, not a peer — what it does and does not measure, and the
per-row caveats that move its numbers, are in [`bench/c/README.md`](bench/c/README.md).
**Go** (added 2026-09-16) is a full column and a peer of sorts: compiled ahead of time, garbage
collected, with its own scheduler — the point between C and .NET the field was missing. Its
judgement calls (panic/recover on the error rows, `iter.Seq` stages on `pipeline`) are in
[`bench/go/README.md`](bench/go/README.md).

**<sup>a</sup> Algorithmic asymmetry, against Brood.** `primes`: most languages hoist a `sqrt`
bound where Brood/Clojure re-test `(* d d) > m` each step. `strings`: Brood/Elixir join the
range directly.

**`mandelbrot`** once read 3.5× slow from two port bugs (exact-rational division, and `y0`
recomputed per pixel), not from the runtime. Both fixed; history in the brood devlog. It then
halved again at the 2026-09-21 refresh (161 → 77 ms wall), and that one WAS the runtime: brood
ADR-378 re-tiers an arm whose floats arrive through vector reads instead of latching it off the
native tier — see FRONTIER.md.

**`collatz` nearly doubled between the 2026-08-27 and 2026-08-28 runs (95 → 185 ms), and the
runtime did not regress.** The port had to move off bare `rem`/`quot`/`max`, which the namespacing
waves retired, onto qualified `math/*` — and one of the three it moved to is **variadic**. Isolated
on one binary: all three qualified **223 ms**; the same with `%max` called directly **142 ms**; all
three primitives **142 ms**. The middle equals the bottom, so `math/rem` and `math/quot` are free
(a fixed-arity one-primitive body is inlined into its caller — `steps` lowers to native with no
`Call` instruction at all) and the whole delta is `math/max`, which is `(apply %max xs)` and cannot
be. Qualification itself costs nothing: bare via `(:use math)` measured 204 ms against 205 ms.
A brood-side A/B across `v0.14.1..HEAD` reads `collatz` flat. See [`FRONTIER.md`](FRONTIER.md) —
the lever is variadic dispatch, not wrappers in general.

**<sup>c</sup> Clojure runs cold.** A fresh JVM per run (~0.34 s) never fully JIT-compiles the
hot loop; a long-running service would beat every number in its column.

**<sup>p</sup> Precompiled.** Elixir, .NET and Go run as prebuilt artifacts (Go as one static binary per row, the way C is built); the rest compile from
source each run. Favours Elixir/.NET, and is the fair analog of `node app.js`. Elixir is
precompiled to `_build` for a specific reason worth knowing: `elixir file.exs` recompiles the
module every run, ~100 ms that lands in *compute* because the `startup` baseline compiles nothing
and so does not subtract it.

**Brood is on the compile-from-source side of that line, and pays it twice.** It compiles the
benchmark program (~1.7 ms, measured) *and* re-evaluates every `std/` module the program
`require`s, on every run — measured per run at `json` **4.6 ms**, `regex` **4.9 ms**, `seq`
**3.2 ms**, `encoding` **2.1 ms**, `os` **0.8 ms**. Like Elixir's ~100 ms, none of it is
subtracted, because the `startup` row loads only `io`. Against this run's compute that is ~2–4%
on the codec rows and ~1% elsewhere — so it does not change any ordering here, but it is a real
handicap and the direction is always against Brood.

**Closed as of the next run: the Brood column now gets the stdlib image, the way Elixir gets
`elixirc`.** The image (brood ADR-218/256) materialises a `require`d module's bindings instead of
re-evaluating its source — `json` 6.5 → 1.7 ms, `http` 12.0 → 3.6 ms, `regex` 4.7 → 1.1 ms,
`datetime` 3.2 → 1.0 ms — and the `json` row measures **−5.6%** end to end.

This is not a thumb on the scale, and the distinction is worth stating: Brood installs the image
**by default**, so it is what every user's `require` already does. What the runtime deliberately
does not do is *build* it (~1 s, which would land on exactly the short-lived runs it exists to help);
`nest` writes it during ordinary project work. A benchmark host might never have run `nest`, so
without a build step the column would measure the source path on one machine and the image on
another. `build_brood()` in the harness removes that split — the same reason `build_beam()` exists,
and the same reason the note above says Elixir is precompiled. Numbers published *before* this
change still carry the per-run library cost described above.

*Correction, 2026-08-27:* an earlier revision of this note said the image left `datetime/now`
**unbound** and failed 150 of ~4900 tests. Both are withdrawn. `datetime/now` has never existed —
the module defines `utc-now` — and the failure counts (150 of 4920, and 170 of 4888 before it) were
measured by installing the image from a *program*, which cannot exercise it: a qualified name
auto-requires its module at compile time, so the test framework loads the library from source before
the first line runs. That configuration materialises **zero** modules while reporting 99 sections
installed. Measured at boot the gap was 157 of 4917, and 112 of those were a concurrency race in the
loader rather than a registration gap.

**Warming the JIT across runs is deliberately *not* done, for Brood or anyone.** Every JIT column
here cold-starts per process — V8, RyuJIT, BeamAsm and HotSpot all re-tier in each new process, and
Clojure carries a caveat (<sup>c</sup>) rather than a warm-up for exactly that reason. The harness's
one discarded run per language warms only what genuinely carries across processes; for Brood that is
the build-id-keyed boot cache, without which a first run costs ~1.2 s instead of ~18 ms. Warming
Brood's *tiering* between measured runs would favour Brood alone, since no other column can be
warmed the same way.

### Immutable structures vs mutable buffers

Two comparisons under one name: Brood/Elixir/Clojure use **persistent** structures, the rest
mutate a buffer in place. Brood has no mutable data at all (ADR-026) except `Table`, an opaque
deep-copying store used by `sieve`. `sort` sits here because memory splits on exactly that line
(124–191 MB vs 25–67 MB) — in the like-for-like table it read as a Brood defect rather than the
price of the guarantee.

**Brood against its actual peers** — the three languages that make the same guarantee:

### In-language codecs vs native libraries

Here Brood has no peer group, and that *is* the result: it runs its own `std/` codecs written
in Brood, while every other column calls a C, JVM or .NET native implementation. The row
measures the library, not the VM. Sizes are small precisely because Brood is slow here, so the
native columns finish in single-digit ms and the ordering *among them* is meaningless.

| benchmark | Go <sup>p</sup> | Node | Ruby | Python | Elixir <sup>p</sup> | .NET <sup>p</sup> | Brood | Clojure <sup>c</sup> | Brood rank |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `json` <sup>n</sup> | 2ms | 2ms | 5ms | 8ms | 7ms | 43ms | **90ms** | 398ms | 7/8 |
| `regex` <sup>n</sup> | 4ms | 4ms | 7ms | 13ms | 18ms | 12ms | **55ms** | 134ms | 7/8 |
| `base64` <sup>n</sup> | &lt;1ms | 4ms | 8ms | 14ms | 12ms | 4ms | **48ms** | 159ms | 7/8 |

**Two of these three moved, and only two.** `json` **166 → 104 ms** and `base64` **91 → 67 ms**:
`string/->codepoints` is a native that had **no native inverse**, so every parser in `std/` rebuilt
its result with `(apply str (map int->char cs))` — a closure call and a one-character string per
code point. `%codepoints->string` is that inverse (brood ADR-249), and `base64`'s decoder also
stopped probing a CHAMP map and calling `nth` per character. `regex` **134 → 106 ms** moved for an
unrelated reason (the boot change — see [Memory and startup](#memory-peak-rss-and-startup)) and
does **not** have this problem at all: its hot path is a memoised DFA whose steady state is one
`table/get`, not string assembly. These are still in-language codecs against native ones, so the
shape of this table is unchanged — the gap is just smaller for two of its rows.

**<sup>n</sup> Denominator at the noise floor.** Read Brood's absolute number, not the ratio.
This is the one ordered table with **no `vs best` column**, deliberately: a rating here would be
Brood-in-Brood against a C/JVM/.NET library, which says nothing about the VM. The denominator is
also unreliable — on a precompiled column whose boot dominates, `compute = wall − startup` can
subtract almost the whole cell away.

### Concurrency — only two of these are the same thing

Brood and Elixir run **preemptively-scheduled isolated processes with copying sends**: a
receiver cannot observe the sender's later mutations, and no unit can starve another. Everything
else here is coroutines on an event loop, OS threads, promises or tasks — cheaper because they
provide less, not because they are better at the same thing.

Against its actual peer:

Brood is never last above; it **is** last on `spawn-live`, below. Note the tables above are the
eleven single-threaded compute rows — the overview chart in the README aggregates the 15 rows
every column implements, where Brood sits 4th of eight. The field drifts ±10%
run-to-run, so read orderings, not digits. (`spawn-live`, `supervisor` and `latency` are outside
the field-wide aggregate: subset of languages, and `latency` is percentiles.)

**That 15 is down from 27, and the reference moved from .NET to C, both on 2026-08-14** when the C
floor column landed. Because the aggregate covers the rows *every* column implements, a partial
column narrows it for everyone — so the field-wide figure is not comparable with runs before that
date. The per-row tables and the trend chart are, since they compare each row against its own
history.

**`supervisor` runs two languages and the absence is the point.** An OTP-style supervisor — links
its children, is told when one exits, restarts per a strategy and an intensity budget — exists as
a *runtime* facility only in Brood and Elixir. Elsewhere it would be a loop this repo wrote, which
measures the harness author.

**`supervisor` +50% at the 2026-09-14 field run — it was the type checker, and it is fixed
(2026-09-15).** The row read **1.33 s against the 0.27.2 column's 886 ms**, verified both ways
(three invocations per side, spreads under 0.6%) with peak RSS unmoved — the first clue that it cost
time and not allocation. It was not the supervisor and not per-child: a `BENCH_N` sweep put it at a
flat ~520 ms of *load* time, and a two-line file calling `supervisor/start` reproduced it. `brood
file.blsp` type-checks a program before running it, and two checker bugs stacked on that file. The
first (brood KI-138): the call-site specializer never memoized a negative answer, so it re-walked the
same question at every call site — the prelude's `get` re-typed 1864 times for 52 distinct
questions. The second, and the larger (KI-139): a `let`/`do`/`if` whose body the inferencer could not
type fell through to the *call* path and was typed as a call to a function named `let`, its bindings
and body re-typed as arguments — every unknown-typed level doubling the walk beneath it, 2^12 on one
239-node body. Two guards now meter the checker's walks and its visits per walk. The `c813ce1a`
refresh read the row at **861 ms** (min of 3, spread 2.1%), under the 886 it started from; the
same-day control (the 0.27.2 column's binary, its image rebuilt, through the same harness) read
975 ms, the box being uniformly ~7% slower that day than on that column's day. The 0.28.0 refresh
later the same day (this column) reads it at 836 ms (spread 0.4%).

`ring` read 835 ms in the `c813ce1a` refresh against 790 published, which looked like a movement
and was not one: the 0.27.2 column's own binary, run through the harness the same day **with its
std image in place**, read 870 ms against its published 795 (+9.5%), and every compute row it was
run on read +5–10% — the box, not the code; the fixed binary was at parity or ahead of it on all
seven rows the same day (ring −4.1%). An earlier version of this note cited a control of 818 /
838 ms that was invalid: the cache keeps only the four newest std images and that binary's had
been evicted, so it was loading the standard library from source. Check `BROOD_IMAGE_TRACE=1`
before trusting a PATH-override control. The 0.28.0 refresh (this column, three invocations
agreeing to ~1–4% on every row) reads ring at 770 ms and every compute row 3–8% under the
`c813ce1a` column — the same box-level shift going back the other way, uniform across rows
that share no code path, so it is read as the plateau and not as a change in 0.28.0.

**Reading a movement.** Table deltas under ~5% are drift on this hardware. Treat any movement as
unproven until a fixed-baseline A/B against the row's own noise floor agrees — that rule has so far
rejected three apparent swings and confirmed two. `spawn-live` is the worst offender: it has
wandered ~20% between whole harness invocations with no code change in between.

**Base RSS is bimodal**, depending only on whether the boot cache is populated — a cold
expanded-prelude boot has measured ~19 MB above the warm figure. That swing, not any code change,
is what the wide historical spread tracks, so read small movements as drift and compare only warm
against warm. Binary size does not imply footprint either: brotli added 1.2 MB of binary and
**zero** RSS. (For the current level, and the one movement that *is* a real regression, see
[Memory and startup](#memory-peak-rss-and-startup).)

**Brood vs Elixir** is the one end-to-end like-for-like column — the only other runtime here with
both persistent structures and isolated preemptive processes. Brood leads `pfib` (1.7×) and `http`
(3.8×); Elixir leads `spawn` (1.4×), `ring` (3.1×), `pingpong` (3.0×) and `supervisor` (1.9× at
the 1b9befd0 refresh, from 3.4× four refreshes earlier — see FRONTIER's notes: the row was
never about the supervisor; its steps were the map primitives, the multi-pair `assoc`
unroll, and now the VM→native direct call's nested-handoff fix and the pre-flight verdict
cache).

**The `pingpong`/`ring` gap IS per-message fixed cost, decomposed 2026-08-30** (an earlier
version of this paragraph claimed otherwise from a stale micro-measurement — the row itself is
the honest meter: `pingpong`'s compute over its 100k round trips is ~865 ns/message against
BEAM's ~265). Two mechanical slices came out that day — an unconditional futex wake per
delivery (−19.7%) and a quasiquote that kept `receive` expansion on the tree-walker (−4%) —
and the profiled remainder splits three ways: the receive loop is structurally *interpreted*
(a `receive` suspends, so its arm can never JIT — the `%receive` fence; ~16% of the row), a
full capture-park/wake/matcher-reactivation cycle per message (~16% across `run_one` +
`receive_match` + enqueue), and the copying send. The recorded levers are brood's
compute-frontier §7.3 (receive as a native exit) and runtime-frontier's per-message list.
`latency`'s tail was a different animal — spawn-to-first-instruction scheduling; fixing that
moved p50 27 → 16 µs without touching the message path.

The mailbox-backlog cliff underneath is **closed**: a `receive` pinned on a fresh `ref` starts its
scan past every message that predates the ref, making request/reply O(1) in the backlog rather than
O(backlog) — 4 µs against 262 µs at a 32,000-message backlog (ADR-195). It cost `pingpong` and
`ring` ~2–3%, which they pay without seeing the benefit since they run near-empty mailboxes.

## `latency` — what a server actually feels like

Every other concurrency row is **closed loop** — the generator waits for each reply, so a stall
makes it politely stop sending and never enters the numbers (coordinated omission). This row is
**open loop**: request *i* is scheduled at `start + i × (1s / 20,000)` whether the system keeps up
or not, and latency is measured from that instant, so queueing delay lands in the number. Every
20th request occupies ~500 µs of CPU; the percentiles cover the other 95%. Offered load is 0.5 of
12 cores, so the tail is scheduling, not saturation.

<!-- BEGIN LATENCY (generated by bench/docs.py) -->
| | p50 | **p99** | p99.9 | max | cores | CPU·s | peak RSS | vs best (p99) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Elixir** | 7 µs | **54 µs** | 66 µs | 213 µs | 2.0× | 5.46 | 79 MB | −1.6× |
| **Brood** | 19 µs | **84 µs** | 909 µs | 2,462 µs | 3.3× | 8.40 | 390 MB | +1.6× |
| **Go** | 76 µs | **104 µs** | 106 µs | 167 µs | 1.8× | 4.42 | 7 MB | +1.9× |
| **Python** | 3 µs | **423 µs** | 479 µs | 959 µs | 1.0× | 2.52 | 11 MB | +7.8× |
| **Node** | 1 µs | **450 µs** | 643 µs | 850 µs | 1.0× | 2.55 | 58 MB | +8.3× |
| **.NET** | 4 µs | **629 µs** | 12,760 µs | 14,945 µs | 2.3× | 5.98 | 48 MB | +11.6× |
<!-- END LATENCY -->

**.NET has the best median and the worst tail by 20×** — p50 4 µs, p99.9 12.8 ms, a 3,196×
spread against Elixir's 10×, while spending the most CPU of any port. "Fast in benchmarks, janky
in production" is what that profile looks like, and no other row here can see it.

**Node and Python, single-threaded, tail better than .NET on twelve cores.** Their p99 (~470 µs)
*is* the fat request's own duration: you wait behind exactly one handler, and it stops there.

**Elixir is what the BEAM claims to be** — 7 / 51 / 87 µs: reduction-counted preemption stops a
500 µs handler holding a scheduler, and per-process heaps keep a collection local.

**Brood is second** — p50 18 µs, p99 **82 µs**, within ~31 µs of the BEAM, and multiples ahead of
third. The *level* is what earlier runs bought: p99 came 439 → 82 over six runs. Two gains were
scheduler placement; the third was ADR-215 removing ~8 µs of compilation from every process's
*arrival* path — **a tail can be dominated by one-off setup that throughput rows amortise away.**
Percentiles on an open-loop row move more than this between invocations, so read the ranking, not
the digits; the p99.9 (280 µs) is not resolvable at this sample size and no claim rests on it.

The scheduler side: children spawn onto the spawner's own worker, so a dispatcher that keeps
running parks every handler behind it for a quantum. An idle worker now learns immediately that a
peer queued a child (it used to re-probe on a 10 ms timer), with brief first refusal for the owner
so a spawn-then-block parent keeps its child on a warm cache. The remaining gap to Elixir is the
median, and it is **not** per-message cost — a send + receive is 1.1 µs measured directly.

**What this row does not claim.** Handlers are CPU-bound, the hard case; a production Node or
Python service would offload that work. It measures runtimes, not frameworks — no HTTP server, no
router, no serialization. "sustained" confirms every port held the 20,000/s schedule
(19,924–20,000/s), and each calibrates its own fat request to ~500 µs and reports what it achieved
(494–526 µs), so a mis-calibration is visible rather than silent.

## `spawn-live` — 300,000 units held alive, each sent a copied message

Holds **300,000 concurrent units alive at once**, then wakes each individually with a
message it must **copy**, and collects each reply through a queue the parent drains one at a
time. Both halves matter: on the BEAM and in Brood `send` copies, so a receiver cannot
observe the sender's later mutations, and the reply is a *message*, not a return value.

**Only two of the five runtimes here provide the same thing**, so the peer comparison comes
first and the rest is context — the same split the concurrency rows use above.

### Against the only other runtime with the same guarantees

<!-- BEGIN PEER (generated by bench/docs.py) -->
| | compute | peak RSS | cores | CPU·s | vs best |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Elixir** (BEAM process) | 662 ms | 924 MB | 2.2× | 1.87 | −1.7× |
| **Brood** (green process) | 1.14 s | 1.48 GB | 3.0× | 3.44 | +1.7× |
<!-- END PEER -->

**Still Brood's worst row: 1.9× slower and 1.9× heavier than the BEAM.**

What's left is the process itself — mailbox, isolated heap, captured continuation. Two candidates
once named here as the top item have since been measured and **withdrawn**: *per-process inline
caches* (on the VM a cached callee resolves no faster than an uncached one — ~2 µs of a 33 µs
unit), and the **receive machinery**, sized at +8.7 µs/unit by a 2026-08-06 decomposition and then
cut to **~1.8%, inside the noise**, by an interleaved three-pattern run on 2026-08-10. The effect
is real — a `receive` matching a literal misses the JIT's native fast frame — but that is not what
the row costs.

What remains, in order: the **process floor** (untouched by any recent win; peak RSS sits flat
near 1.6–1.7 GB throughout) and the cold call into `fold`, now larger than the fold it performs.
`(hibernate)` returns most of a process's memory explicitly. See [FRONTIER.md](FRONTIER.md).

### The coroutine runtimes, for context

A promise, an `asyncio` task and a .NET `Task` are closures on a **shared** heap: no isolated
heap, no mailbox, and nothing to preempt. They are cheap because they provide less, not
because they are better at the same thing.

<!-- BEGIN COROUTINE (generated by bench/docs.py) -->
| | compute | peak RSS | cores | CPU·s | vs best |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Node** (promise) | 215 ms | 247 MB | 2.2× | 0.52 | −1.2× |
| **.NET** (`Task`) | 261 ms | 138 MB | 1.6× | 0.46 | +1.2× |
| **Go** (goroutine) | 466 ms | 847 MB | 2.2× | 1.05 | +2.2× |
| **Python** (`asyncio` task) | 1.25 s | 361 MB | 1.0× | 1.26 | +5.8× |
<!-- END COROUTINE -->

Two defects here were fixed on 2026-07-30 and the result surprised: .NET's
`TaskCompletionSource` resumed inline on the setter's thread (1000 of 1000, none on the pool), so
"wake 300k units" was 300k synchronous calls; and all three collected results into a pre-allocated
array rather than paying for a second copied message. Forcing .NET to schedule made it *faster*
(345 → 294 ms), so the credit these runtimes get is largely earned — what they do not provide is
structural, priced by the guarantees above rather than the clock. Python still runs at **1.0
cores**: it holds 300k units by never running two.

### The isolated primitive, where each runtime has one

Each runtime's *isolated* primitive does not reach this scale, so it was measured small and
projected: Node's `worker_thread` is linear at ~11.4 MB / ~5.3 ms per unit → **~3.4 TB** at 300k;
Ruby's threads are ~21 KB each but quadratic in time (1.26 s at 5k, 20.78 s at 20k) → **over an
hour**.

**The payload is a contiguous sequence in every port** (a Brood vector, a BEAM tuple, arrays
elsewhere) — it was a 16-element cons list in Brood and Elixir until 2026-07-30, charging the two
process runtimes 16 pointer-chased copies for the same 16 integers. Measured under the harness,
Brood only: **11% faster and 0.6% lighter** with the vector.

The split is the interesting part: representation moved *time* and left *memory* untouched, so the
GB is not the messages — it is the process floor (~5.5 KB × 300,000).

## Memory (peak RSS) and startup

- **Base RSS**: Brood **51 MB** — 6th of eight, behind C (1.7), Python (9.7), Ruby (19), .NET (26)
  and Node (43), ahead of Elixir (73) and Clojure (104). Brood stays light *relative to itself*
  across the suite; the exceptions are the allocation-heavy rows (`supervisor` ~600 MB,
  `spawn-live` 1.7 GB). The [standings table](README.md#readme) carries the current figures.
- **Startup**: Brood **13 ms** — 3rd of eight, behind only C (2.0) and Python (10.1), and ahead of
  Node (17.9), .NET (22), Ruby (39), Elixir (180) and Clojure (335).

**Startup halved this run, and it is the one figure to read as a result rather than a ranking.**
It was **31 ms** and is **18 ms** — 5th of eight to 4th, and now within 0.5 ms of Node. The cause
was **KI-61**: each namespacing wave that moved prelude names into a module forced that module to
load *from source* at every boot, because the prelude's qualified refs are late-bound and boot's
namespace-resolve does not auto-require for the root prelude — `(require-one 'string)` +4.0 ms and
`(require-one 'seq)` +7.5 ms, and a per-wave tax with no end. The fix was not the std-image
registration replay this file used to name: the prelude's references into those modules are now
**autoload stubs** that load on first call, so boot loads nothing and the next wave costs one
declaration (brood ADR-246). A second half went with it — the warm boot also read the prelude a
*second* time, positioned, only to recover def-sites for editor navigation; those now travel in
the boot cache (ADR-247). Base RSS fell 56 → 52 MB with them, and prelude boot itself is ~7.5 ms
against 22.8 ms before.

**That fix is also why almost every other row improved, and the mechanism is worth stating**
because it contradicts the obvious prediction. `compute = wall − startup`, so a saving that shows
up in both should cancel — but the `startup` row is `(io/puts 0)`, which loads `io` and through it
`string`, while most rows load neither. Those rows keep the *whole* lazy-load saving while only
~13 ms of it is subtracted away: `fib`'s wall fell 29 ms against `startup`'s 13. So the −12% to
−20% across the compute tables is one boot change being counted once per row, not twenty
independent wins.

**The two codec rows are separate and are real.** `json` **166 → 104 ms** and `base64`
**91 → 67 ms**, both from removing per-element work rather than per-invocation work:
`string/->codepoints` had no native inverse, so every parser in `std/` rebuilt its result with
`(apply str (map int->char cs))` — a closure call and a one-character string per code point
(brood ADR-249) — and `base64`'s decoder additionally stopped probing a CHAMP map and calling
`nth` for every character. Both were confirmed by fixed-baseline A/B before this run
(json −20.8% and base64 −9.5% on wall, against sub-1% floors). `regex` **134 → 106 ms** is *not*
a codec win — it measured flat under A/B, and its improvement here is the boot change above.

**Read the scoreboard's movement with care this run: Brood's like-for-like score went 6.97 → 7.23
while every one of its rows got faster.** That is the field moving, not Brood. The score is a
geomean of each column against the row's best, so it is sensitive to what happened to the other
seven — and `compute = wall − startup` is brutal on a column whose startup dominates. Elixir's
startup barely moved (185 → 183.5 ms) but its `bintree` *compute* reads 37 → 8 ms, because compute
there is the difference of two ~190 ms numbers: a 13% change in its wall becomes a 77% change in
its compute. Four of Elixir's rows behave that way, which is enough to move the whole geomean and
Brood's rank with it. **Cross-run aggregate comparisons are not reliable at this magnitude**; the
per-row Brood figures, which subtract only an 18 ms startup from a 70–190 ms wall, are.

Both figures are the warm steady state — the build-id-keyed boot cache is populated (a fresh
binary's first run costs more), which the harness's warmup keeps out of both columns.

## How to read it

- **Aggregate**: the [scoreboard](#scoreboard)'s `Like-for-like` row — the geomean over the 15
  rows every column implements, C = 1.00 — is the figure, and it is regenerated each run rather
  than restated here. The field drifts ±10% run-to-run, so the ordering is the claim, not the
  digits. It says nothing about behaviour under load — that is what `latency` is for.
- **A single harness sample cannot separate a result from drift.** `spawn-live`'s real moves were
  −16% and −9%, each with a counted cause; two earlier swings on the same row, `spawn` +20% and
  `spawn-live` −22%, measured −3.6% and −2.0% under A/B and were nothing. Same row, same
  magnitude, opposite verdicts — only the A/B tells them apart, and it is symmetric: it has
  deflated good news and confirmed bad.
- **`nbody`** is the cautionary case: the JIT types an arm's *parameters* only, so a function whose
  floats arrive from a `def`'d constant lowered its float multiply onto the integer path and
  deopted on every activation until the sixteen-deopt rule bailed it to the interpreter.
  Self-healing hid it — a deopt storm became silent interpretation.
- **Where Brood is weakest**: `matmul` and `nqueens` (the two largest like-for-like gaps),
  `json`/`regex`/`base64` (in-language codecs against native ones), `pipeline` (lazy-seq churn the
  JIT doesn't cover) and `bintree` (four non-tail calls per node — the open watch-item).

The per-language source for every benchmark lives under [`bench/`](bench/), eight files per
benchmark named identically except the extension, so the implementations diff side by side. Run
the suite with `python3 bench/harness.py` (see the [README](README.md#running-it) for options).
